Does consensus under-reaction grow with the size of the news? Three preregistered tests on the US SPF, the ECB SPF and the Livingston Survey

[Author]

November 2026

Abstract

When the consensus of professional forecasters revises a forecast, the outturn tends to land beyond the new number: the consensus under-reacts. This note asks whether it under-reacts more after large news. Three preregistered tests answer on three surveys and two continents: the US Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF, targets 1969–2026), the ECB SPF (2000–2025) and the Livingston Survey (1947–2026). Large news is defined from the data surprise released before the survey, not from the revision, because sorting on the revision creates the effect through survey noise. The consensus under-reacts in all three surveys: the slope of the forecast error on the forecast revision is 0.19, 0.37 and 0.37, in standard deviations. The extra slope after large news is −0.03, −0.11 and −0.12, and every 90% interval contains zero. The predicted +0.40 is excluded in the two conclusive tests (upper bounds 0.05 and 0.11), which are eliminated. The US test is formally inconclusive: a schema guard failed on one row that enters no regression. A separate pipeline rebuilt every sealed verifier number from raw public data.

1 Introduction

A forecaster under-reacts when news moves the forecast in the right direction but not far enough. The standard measure is the slope of the forecast error (outturn minus forecast) on the forecast revision (new minus older forecast for the same target), as in Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2015). If the forecast used all its information, the revision could not predict the error, and the slope would be zero. A positive slope means under-reaction: after an upward revision, the outturn ends up higher still.

The consensus of professional forecasters is known to under-react on average. This note asks a narrower question: is the under-reaction stronger after large news? If it were, a big data surprise would leave the consensus further behind than a small one. The 2021–2022 inflation surge made the question natural: forecasters revised up, and inflation kept beating them.

The answer matters to two kinds of readers. A rates or macro desk uses the consensus as the benchmark against which data are read. If the consensus lagged more after large surprises, the size of the last surprise would tell the desk how stale the consensus is. A central bank that reads survey expectations needs to know whether their sluggishness depends on the size of shocks.

This note reports three tests. Each was preregistered and sealed by a SHA-256 hash before any statistic was computed. Each verdict was applied by code to numbers recomputed by an independent verifier. A separate pipeline then rebuilt every number from raw public data. The answer, in three sentences:

  1. Consensus forecasts under-react on average in all three surveys: the slope of the error on the revision is 0.19 in the US SPF, 0.37 in the ECB SPF and 0.37 in the Livingston Survey.
  2. The under-reaction does not grow after large news: the extra slope after large news is −0.03, −0.11 and −0.12.
  3. The predicted extra slope of +0.40 is excluded in the two conclusive tests (ECB SPF and Livingston), while the first test, on the US SPF, is formally inconclusive because a schema guard failed on a row outside every regression.

All slopes are in standard deviations of error per standard deviation of revision. The US base slope is descriptive; the other two are preregistered positive controls.

2 How the question arose

An AI-assisted pipeline. The question came out of an AI-agent research pipeline run under a fixed protocol. In each generation, agents from four model families (Kimi, Gemini, OpenAI Astra and Claude) each proposed five idea cards in a closed format: a falsifiable hypothesis, a numerical prediction and a test that would kill it. Judges from the same four families ranked the twenty cards on anonymised copies; code sealed before the judging aggregated their ranks, and the top five went on. For each retained card an agent checked novelty, recording the sources it had opened, and tested access to the data. Ideas that survived their tests became parents of the next generation.

The K20 card. One parent of the third generation was J02, a test on ECB staff inflation projections. Their errors two quarters ahead follow revisions (standardised slope 0.443 over 1999–2026), but the slope falls to 0.050 when 2021–2022 is removed. J02 rests on one large shock. A Claude-family proposer asked the next question: is under-reaction a property of large shocks? The US SPF has five variables and several large shocks since the late 1960s, so each episode can be removed in turn. The card (K20) predicted a base slope of about +0.3 and an extra slope of about +0.40 (range +0.2 to +0.6) when the standardised revision exceeds one standard deviation. It framed this as “reluctance to make large revisions”, against models in which attention rises with large shocks and the interaction is negative. K20 ranked second of twenty in the aggregate. Two of the three judges from other families ranked it third, the Gemini judge tenth; three of the four judges put it on their short list, none on their discard list. The judges’ scores for interest and contribution were high, for novelty low (2 or 3 out of 5).

The novelty check and the judges’ flaws. The novelty check classed K20 as a “variant”. The base slope was published long ago, and so was its dependence on periods and states, but no estimate of the extra slope after large news on the SPF consensus was found. The check corrected the card on data (growth rates instead of base-dependent levels; CPI and the T-bill start in 1981) and stressed its main flaw, also named by two judges: a large revision is not a large exogenous piece of news, and sorting on the revision creates the interaction through survey noise, in the direction of the hypothesis (Section 4.3).

The first test, and why it ended inconclusive. The K20 preregistration answered these flaws. “Large” became the top third of the data surprise released between the two surveys; constants, class effects and base slopes became variable-specific; a floor for mechanical bias and an episode guard entered the rule. K20 ended inconclusive. Schema check 9 failed on one row, CPI 2026-Q1: October 2025 is missing in FRED (no data were collected during the federal shutdown), so the previous-quarter CPI level is missing. That row has no outturn and enters no regression. The estimate itself was c = −0.030, 90% interval [−0.146, 0.086].

Decisive instruments. The project lead then asked that the next tests be decisive. Two requests reached the writer of the first replication while it was being drafted: a positive control, so that a null extra slope could not be the silence of an instrument that sees nothing; and a simulation, before sealing, showing that the full rule reaches a decision with probability of at least 0.80 both when the true extra slope is 0 and when it is +0.40. The writer also fixed K20’s faulty guard: schema checks count for the verdict only on the rows that enter the computation; failures elsewhere are reported apart.

Two blind replications. The same question was then asked on two more surveys: K20-ZE on the ECB SPF and K20-LIV on the Livingston Survey. Their writers knew K20’s result and the literature but had seen no statistic from the new survey. They kept K20’s statistic, thresholds and floor formula, and adapted the data definitions. The Livingston Survey publishes individual answers, so its preregistration replaced K20’s assumed noise share by a measured one.

How an economist could have had the idea. No AI was needed to ask this. The error-on-revision regression is a standard tool, and its state dependence is already debated: rigidity falls in turbulent periods (Coibion and Gorodnichenko, 2015), and in rational-inattention models attention rises when shocks are large and visible (Baker, McElroy and Sheng, 2020, after natural disasters). After 2021–2022 the obvious question is: is a big surprise absorbed more slowly than a small one? An economist would add one interaction term to the standard regression. The less obvious step, which the judges and the novelty check supplied here, is to define “big” from the data surprise and not from the revision itself.

3 Related work

The base slope. Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2015) regress the consensus error on the consensus revision and read a positive slope as information rigidity; they apply it to the US SPF, the Livingston Survey and other surveys. Bordalo, Gennaioli, Ma and Shleifer (2020) run it on the SPF consensus with targets three quarters ahead. In their Table 3 (2018 version), in points of error per point of revision: unemployment 0.82 (se 0.21), 3-month T-bill 0.71 (0.26), GDP deflator inflation 1.21 (0.21), real GDP 0.45 (0.25). On the ECB SPF, Broer and Kohlhas (2024) find a consensus slope of 0.740 (0.406) for HICP inflation over 2000Q1–2020Q1. The base slope is therefore not new here; it serves as a positive control.

State dependence. Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2015, Sections 4.2–4.3 of the working paper) find that rigidity fell as volatility rose from the late 1960s to the early 1980s, and fell a few quarters into recessions, with little rigidity after 11 September 2001. Kučinskas and Peters (2024) find more under-reaction of the SPF inflation consensus when inflation is high and less in recessions, which they attribute to the persistence of inflation. Baker, McElroy and Sheng (2020) find, in Consensus Economics forecasts for 54 countries, that information rigidity falls sharply after large unexpected natural disasters. Baley, Turén and Bordini (2026) find that revisions are more frequent and larger in volatile times. Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2012) show that in the sticky-information model the normalised response of the error does not depend on the volatility of the shock. All of these condition on periods or states, not on the size of the news.

Size of the news. de Silva, Larsen-Hallock, Rej and Thesmar (2025) find a strongly non-linear relation between error and revision in firms’ sales forecasts: forecasters under-react to ordinary news and over-react to very large news. That is the interaction asked here, with the opposite sign to the card’s hypothesis, on firm data rather than macroeconomic data.

The gap. The novelty check searched for an estimate of the extra slope after large news on the US SPF consensus and found none; that is not proof that none exists. The two replications add the same statistic on the ECB SPF and the Livingston Survey. The literature leans against the hypothesis tested: only the high-inflation result of Kučinskas and Peters points the same way.

4 Data and design

4.1 Three surveys

All data are public and free. Forecasts come from the Philadelphia Fed (SPF mean and median forecasts; Livingston means, medians and individual answers) and from the ECB (SPF individual answers). Outturns come from the Philadelphia Fed’s Real-Time Data Set for Macroeconomists (first releases of the GDP deflator and real GDP), FRED (latest vintage of unemployment, CPI, interest rates and housing starts) and Eurostat (euro-area HICP, real GDP and monthly unemployment). The project README lists every file and URL. The consensus is the mean forecast; the median is a secondary analysis.

4.2 The regression

Within each test, the error and the revision are standardised by series on the main sample: by variable in the US SPF and Livingston tests, by variable × horizon (six series) in the ECB SPF test. Call them ze and zr, and let L = 1 after large news. The main regression, by OLS, is

ze = ∑gαgDg + ∑gδgDgL + ∑gbgDgzr + c zrL + u,

where Dg indicates series g. Each series has its own constant, its own class effect and its own base slope bg: the slope after small news. The slope after large news is bg + c. The extra slope c is common to all series; it is the primary statistic. A single common slope would confuse a non-linearity with differences between variables, and an interaction without its own class effect would credit a level difference to the slope. The base slope drops L: one constant per series and one common slope, the Coibion–Gorodnichenko regression in standardised units.

4.3 What counts as large news, and why not the revision

The card defined large news as a large revision. The tests do not, for a mechanical reason. The published consensus is the true average forecast plus noise: the panel changes from one survey to the next, and answers are rounded. The noise of the survey being evaluated enters the revision with a plus sign and the error with a minus sign. Two effects follow:

  1. Selection on noise. Sorting on the size of the revision also sorts on the size of that noise. When true news has fatter tails than the noise, a large revision is mostly signal and a small one mostly noise. The slope is pushed down among small revisions and not among large ones, so c > 0 even if the true slope is the same everywhere.
  2. Differential attenuation. Noise of a given size weighs more where true revisions vary less, so it lowers the small-news slope more. This also pushes c up, whatever the sort.

All three tests therefore define large news as the top third of the absolute data surprise of each variable, measured on data released before the survey that makes the revision (Table 1). None of these surprises contains the noise of the forecast being evaluated, which removes effect 1. Effect 2 remains; the floor of Section 4.5 handles it.

The project checked the argument on simulated panels with no true size effect: constant true slope, fat-tailed news (Student t with 3 degrees of freedom), consensus noise in both surveys (about 11% of the revision variance), and a lagged surprise that reveals the period’s volatility but not the noise. Over 300 panels of 1,000 rows, the mean c was −0.003 with the surprise sort and +0.046 with the card’s revision sort when the noise grows with turbulence. When the noise has a fixed size, the two sorts gave +0.050 and +0.120: the surprise sort removes the selection bias, and a smaller residual remains, the differential attenuation (Figure 1, right; descriptive).

4.4 Inference and guards

Standard errors. Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, written from the formula: scores summed by date, then Newey-West with Bartlett weights in calendar time, empty dates counted, no small-sample correction. US SPF: 4 lags by target quarter, critical value 1.645. ECB SPF: 8 lags by survey round, because the error on an annual target contains the news of up to eight rounds, and critical value 1.708 (Student t with 25 degrees of freedom, for about 26 independent target years). Livingston: 2 lags by half-year, one year as in the US test, critical value 1.645.

Episode guard. A survival requires t ≥ 1 for c after removing each episode window in turn. US SPF: seven windows, each NBER recession from peak to trough plus four quarters, with the 2020 recession joined to the 2021–2023 inflation surge. ECB SPF: three euro-area windows dated by the CEPR-EABCN committee (2008Q1–2009Q2, 2011Q3–2013Q1, 2019Q4–2023Q4). Livingston: eleven NBER windows, peak to trough plus 14 months. An effect carried by a single episode cannot survive.

Relevance. Revisions must be at least 1.25 times more variable after large news than after small news; otherwise the sort does not separate large news from small. In the ECB test this guard binds only when survival is not reached, because its decisiveness simulation showed that the ratio can fall below 1 when the hypothesis is true.

Positive control (replications only). ECB SPF: the lower 90% bound of the base slope, or of the mean small-news slope, must be above zero. Livingston: the lower bound of the base slope must be above zero, unless the whole interval of c lies below zero.

Schema checks. Twelve checks on the analysis file. In K20 a failure on any row made the test inconclusive; in the replications only failures on rows in the computation count.

4.5 The mechanical-bias floor

If the true slope is β everywhere, differential attenuation alone produces

cmeca = (2β + k) × (ν / 2) × (1/a − 1/A),

where ν is the share of noise in the variance of the revision, k the ratio of the standard deviations of revision and error, and a and A the variances of the standardised revision after small and large news. β is estimated by the mean small-news slope. A survival requires the whole 90% interval of c to lie above the floor max(0.10, cmeca), not just above zero. The floor was set differently in each test:

  • US SPF. ν was assumed at 0.20, about twice the writer’s central guess (0.02 to 0.12) for a mean of 30 to 40 answers. The bias was 0.081 and the floor 0.10.
  • ECB SPF. The same assumed ν = 0.20. With a variance ratio of 8.42 instead of about 3, the bias was 0.425, and so was the floor.
  • Livingston. ν was measured from the individual answers: for each row, the sampling variance of the two consensus means over the variance of the revision; the median by variable, then the mean over variables: 0.016 (0.010 to 0.025 by variable). Doubled for prudence, it gives a bias of 0.122 and a floor of 0.122. With the assumed 0.20, the same formula would have given 0.784.

The floor enters only the survival condition. Elimination compares the upper bound of c with 0.40, and the mechanical bias pushes c up, not down.

4.6 Verdict rule

Each preregistration fixed three outcomes, applied in this order:

  • Inconclusive if a schema check fails; the sample is below its minimum (1,000, 570 or 540 rows); the relevance guard fails; the positive control fails (replications); the 90% interval of c contains both the floor and 0.40; or the interval is above the floor and reaches 0.40, but removing one episode drops t below 1 with c still positive.
  • Survives if the lower 90% bound of c is above the floor, the upper bound reaches 0.40, and t ≥ 1 without each episode.
  • Eliminated otherwise. In practice, either (a) the upper bound is below 0.40, so the predicted +0.40 is excluded at the one-sided 5% level, or (b) the main test passes but c ≤ 0 without one episode.

5 Protocol

Every test followed one protocol, fixed before any preregistration.

  • Preregistration. A writer agent read the card, the judges’ flaws and the novelty note, then wrote the data sources, the sample, the columns and schema checks of the analysis file, the statistic, the standard errors, the guards, the secondary analyses, the tolerances and the verdict rule, with a machine-readable copy of the rule. It could see file headers, column names, counts of present cells and number formats. It computed no error, revision, surprise or regression; power and decisiveness were simulated without outcome data. The text was then sealed by its SHA-256 hash (Appendix A). Nothing in it changed afterwards.
  • Experimenter. An agent in a fresh session downloaded the data, built the analysis file and computed every field. Deviations and ambiguities went to ecarts.md.
  • Verifier. An agent in a fresh session, on another model, read only the preregistration and the analysis file and recomputed every field with its own code, schema checks included. It did not see the experimenter’s code or numbers.
  • Verdict. A script checked agreement between experimenter and verifier within the preregistered tolerances and applied the sealed rule to the verifier’s numbers. No agent wrote a verdict. A reading written after each verdict explains it and states that it does not change it.

Reproduction. For this note, a separate pipeline (run_all.py) checks each seal, downloads the raw files, rebuilds the three analysis datasets with its own code, recomputes every preregistered field and applies the sealed rules. It reproduces every sealed verifier number within tolerance: 53 of 53 for K20, 65 of 65 for K20-ZE and 63 of 63 for K20-LIV. The largest gap on any field is about 4 × 10⁻¹². The sealed rules applied to the pipeline’s numbers give the sealed verdicts again. The rebuilt ECB SPF and Livingston analysis files are bit-identical to the sealed ones, and every raw file is byte-identical (SHA-256) to the copy the sealed test downloaded.

Every number below comes from results/results.json, results/RESULTS.md or the sealed verifier files. Analyses marked descriptive were added for this note and cannot change a verdict.

Division of labour. Agents proposed, judged, checked novelty, wrote the preregistrations, ran the experiments, verified them and drafted this note. [To be completed by the author: what the author personally decided, wrote, checked or re-derived; the models and versions in each role.]

6.1 The consensus under-reacts in all three surveys

The base slope is positive in every survey: 0.191 (se 0.047) in the US SPF, 0.366 (se 0.057) in the ECB SPF and 0.373 (se 0.067) in the Livingston Survey. In both replications the preregistered positive control passed, with lower 90% bounds of 0.268 and 0.263. A null extra slope is therefore not the silence of an instrument that sees nothing.

Descriptive. By variable, the US slope ranges from −0.12 (real GDP) to 0.36 (T-bill); the ECB slopes are 0.37 (HICP), 0.33 (GDP) and 0.39 (unemployment); the Livingston slopes run from 0.21 (prime rate) to 0.50 (CPI and T-bill). In raw units, the US slopes for unemployment (0.80), the T-bill (0.80) and the deflator (1.11) are close to the 0.82, 0.71 and 1.21 of Bordalo et al. (2020), with a different target definition; real GDP differs (−0.57 against 0.45). The base slope is not stable over time (Figure 2): in the US SPF it is 0.06 in the 1970s and 1980s, 0.32 in the 2000s and 0.01 in the 2010s; in the ECB SPF it falls from 0.40 (targets 2000–2009) to 0.23 (2020–2025).

6.2 Under-reaction does not grow after large news

US SPF (K20): inconclusive. On 1,004 rows, 334 after large surprises, c = −0.030 (se 0.071, t = −0.42), 90% interval [−0.146, 0.086]. The sort worked: revisions were 3.06 times more variable after large surprises. The verdict is inconclusive because schema check 9 failed on CPI 2026-Q1. The preregistration had claimed this check was guaranteed by the structure of the sources, without verifying the last row. The experimenter and the verifier each found the failure and judged the row correct; neither rewrote the check. The row has no outturn, so it is not in the main sample, and removing it changes no estimate. With the check set aside, the same rule applied to the same numbers gives “eliminated” (upper bound 0.086 < 0.40). That is reported for information only, never as the verdict.

ECB SPF (K20-ZE): eliminated. On 578 rows, 196 after large news, c = −0.106 (se 0.090, t = −1.18), 90% interval [−0.259, 0.047]. The schema checks found 0 violations and 0 anomalies elsewhere, and the positive control passed (base slope 0.366; small-news slope 0.447, lower bound 0.298). The upper bound is below 0.40: eliminated, case (a). One ambiguity was found in the text, whether to round surprises before the cut; both roles followed the letter (no rounding), and the rounded reading gives c = −0.099 and the same verdict.

Livingston (K20-LIV): eliminated. On 548 rows, 182 after large news, c = −0.122 (se 0.139, t = −0.88), 90% interval [−0.351, 0.107]. The positive control passed (base slope 0.373, lower bound 0.263), and the measured floor was 0.122. The upper bound is below 0.40: eliminated, case (a).

In all three surveys the slope after large news (0.164, 0.341, 0.321) is below the slope after small news (0.194, 0.447, 0.443), although no difference is significant. Figures 3 and 4 show the answer.

6.3 Robustness

The preregistered secondary analyses were computed whatever the result and cannot change a verdict.

Without each episode. c stays between −0.084 and +0.014 in the US SPF (seven windows; Figure 5), between −0.185 and −0.064 in the ECB SPF (three windows) and between −0.131 and −0.056 in the Livingston Survey (eleven windows). No single episode hides a positive effect.

By variable (Figure 3). No variable has c above 0.40. Four of the thirteen point estimates are positive: US deflator +0.17 (se 0.18), US CPI +0.05 (0.15), ECB HICP +0.13 (0.17) and Livingston unemployment +0.38 (0.29). The other nine are negative, from −0.03 to −0.47. Figure 6 shows the US slopes after small and large surprises side by side.

The pandemic. The preregistrations excluded the 2020–2021 rows of the activity variables before seeing any data, because a handful of targets that moved by several points in one round would outweigh decades. Putting them back gives −0.095 in the US SPF and −0.320 in the Livingston Survey. In the ECB SPF it turns c positive: +0.177 (se 0.077), 90% interval [0.04, 0.31], still below 0.40. Descriptive: the change comes from unemployment (+0.577, se 0.205, with the pandemic rows); HICP is unchanged (+0.127) and GDP gives −0.039.

Size or era. Large surprises cluster in the 1970s and early 1980s, when rigidity was lower (Coibion and Gorodnichenko, 2015). Since 1985, c is −0.067 in the US SPF and −0.039 in the Livingston Survey.

Other choices. With medians, c is 0.075, −0.031 and −0.095. Even the card’s own sort on the revision, which the simulation shows is biased upward, gives −0.003, −0.229 and −0.184. In the ECB SPF, a surprise measured against the consensus instead of the previous figure gives −0.271 (se 0.113, 554 rows), and c is −0.011 for the current year and −0.198 for the next. None of the alternative standard errors would bring an upper bound near 0.40.

7 Limits

  1. The first test is inconclusive. K20’s verdict rests on a guard that failed on a correct row outside every regression. Repairing the guard after seeing the numbers would have defeated the seal, so K20’s “eliminated” remains a reading, not a verdict. The conclusive evidence is the two replications.
  2. The ECB SPF floor was far above the simulated one. The decisiveness simulation assumed K20-like dispersions (variance ratio about 3, floor 0.10). The observed ratio was 8.42 and the floor 0.425. Had the true c been near +0.40, the test would mostly have ended inconclusive, so its simulated probability of deciding under the hypothesis (0.891) was too optimistic. The elimination does not depend on the floor: it comes from the upper bound of c (0.047), which the floor does not enter.
  3. The Livingston dispersions matched the writer’s less favourable scenario. Level targets gave k = 1.02 and a variance ratio of 10.10, not K20’s 0.29 and 3.06. In that scenario (S-b) the preregistration’s simulation eliminated a null effect only 78% of the time (0.778), just under the required 0.80, against 0.936 in the main scenario; a true +0.40 survived 88% of the time. The positive control passed and the test decided. Because the floor was measured (0.122) rather than assumed (0.784), a real +0.40 had a fair chance to survive.
  4. The unemployment lead is post hoc. Unemployment is the only Livingston variable with a positive c (+0.38, se 0.29), and in the ECB SPF the only notable positive sign comes from unemployment once the 2020–2021 targets are put back. This pattern was noticed after the verdicts, on one variable. It is a lead, not a result.
  5. “Eliminated” means “+0.40 excluded”, not “no effect at all”. The tests were built to answer “+0.40 or not”. In the Livingston simulation a true c of 0.20 was eliminated about 7 times in 10. By-variable intervals are wide (Livingston unemployment reaches 0.85). And the tests are about large surprises: a threshold in the size of the revision itself would show only weakly through a surprise sort (K20 preregistration, limit 3).
  6. The tests are not independent experiments. The US SPF and the Livingston Survey cover the same US shocks, and some forecasters answer both. The replication writers knew K20’s result; the Livingston writer read the euro-area test’s commit titles at the end of drafting and changed nothing after.
  7. Standard errors. Driscoll-Kraay errors tend to be too small with few independent periods. In the ECB SPF the effective number of observations (735) exceeds the 578 rows, which the preregistration flags as a sign of a too-small standard error; the 1.708 critical value corrects only part of it. Every alternative in Table 3 still keeps the upper bounds far below 0.40.
  8. Data choices. Most outturns are latest vintages. The Livingston surprise interpolates a straight path; the ECB surprise is a change in the published figure, part of which was predictable (base effects). Both blur the sort and push c towards zero if an effect exists. The pandemic exclusions are choices (S3 undoes them). The ECB positive control was not blind for inflation: an earlier test had found a consensus slope of 0.92.
  9. Scope and review. Each verdict is a one-sided 5% decision under its own rule, with no correction for the other ideas tested in the pipeline. No economist has reviewed this work.

8 What it means, and next steps

Sticky but proportional updating. After large news the consensus revises much more: revisions are 3 to 10 times more variable. But it leaves the same share of the news on the table, or slightly less: the slope after large news (0.16, 0.34, 0.32) is no higher than after small news (0.19, 0.45, 0.44). The consensus moves part of the way whatever the size of the news.

Against “reluctance to make large revisions”. The card’s hypothesis, that forecasters revise too little exactly when they should revise a lot, is rejected wherever the test could decide. ECB staff under-reaction in 2021–2022 (J02) is not the expression of a general rule “the bigger the shock, the bigger the under-reaction” in these three surveys.

What remains compatible. Constant rigidity: sticky or noisy information of a constant degree, in which the normalised response does not depend on the volatility of shocks (Coibion and Gorodnichenko, 2012). Or attention that rises mildly with shocks: c is negative in all three surveys, though never significant (t = −0.42, −1.18 and −0.88). The slopes after large news stay positive, so there is no sign that the consensus over-reacts to large news, as de Silva et al. (2025) find for firms’ sales forecasts.

For a desk. In these samples, the under-reaction of the consensus is a constant-share effect. The size of the last surprise does not signal that the consensus is lagging more than usual. These are in-sample slopes: none of the three tests asks whether they could be used in real time.

Next steps.

  • Individual answers. Build the consensus from the forecasters present in both surveys, as Bordalo et al.
    1. do, from the published individual data. That removes panel-composition noise and would allow a sort on the revision itself; the novelty check also suggests sorting on the previous survey’s revision, which does not share the evaluated noise.
  • The unemployment lead. Test it in a new sealed test, on data not used here, with its own prediction.
  • Real-time use. Ask whether a revision-based correction of the consensus would have helped out of sample.
  • Review. Have an economist review the design and the reading.

Appendix A: Audit trail and reproduction

Audit trail. The sealed records of the three tests are kept byte for byte, in French as written, in audit/K20/, audit/K20-ZE/ and audit/K20-LIV/: the preregistration (preenregistrement.md) and its seal, the verdict computed by code with the verifier’s numbers and the machine-readable rule (verdict.json), the verifier’s numbers (verification.json, replications), the experimenter’s deviations (ecarts.md) and the reading written after the verdict (lecture-apres-coup.md). audit/README.md explains them in English. The seals, recomputed on these copies:

How to reproduce. From the project folder, with Python 3.13 and numpy, pandas, scipy, statsmodels, matplotlib and openpyxl:

python run_all.py      # checks the seals, downloads or reuses the raw files, rebuilds everything
python -m pytest       # estimators, conventions, every sealed number and verdict, the simulation

The first run downloads the raw public files into data/raw/; later runs reuse the cache and take about 35 seconds. run_all.py stops if a preregistration no longer matches its seal. It writes results/results.json (all numbers), results/RESULTS.md (tables and descriptive analyses), results/reproduction.md (sealed against pipeline, field by field) and the six figures.
